question.prompt: Let \(D(n)\) denote the number of ways of writing the positive integer \(n\) as a product \[n = f_1 \cdot f_2 \cdots f_k,\] where \(k \ge 1,\) the \(f_i\) are integers strictly greater than \(1,\) and the order in which the factors are listed matters (that is, two representations that differ only in the order of the factors are counted as distinct). For example, the number \(6\) can be written as \(6,\) \(2 \cdot 3,\) and \(3 \cdot 2,\) so \(D(6) = 3.\) What is \(D(96)?\)

solutions.title: Build 96 from 32
solutions.explanation:
Because \(96=3\cdot32\) contains just one prime factor of \(3\), we can first factor \(32\) and then decide where the \(3\) belongs.

Write \(32=2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2\). An ordered factorization of \(32\) comes from cutting this row into consecutive nonempty groups and multiplying within each group. To obtain \(m\) factors, choose \(m-1\) of the four gaps as cuts. This gives \(\binom{4}{m-1}\) factorizations. Each factor's exponent of \(2\) records its group length, so different cut choices give different ordered factorizations.

For each factorization with \(m\) factors, we can introduce the \(3\) in either of two ways:

- Insert \(3\) as a separate factor in one of the \(m+1\) positions, including the two ends.
- Multiply one of the \(m\) existing factors by \(3\).

Thus there are \(2m+1\) choices. These produce every factorization of \(96\) exactly once: locate its unique factor divisible by \(3\), then either remove it if it equals \(3\), or divide it by \(3\) otherwise. This uniquely recovers the factorization of \(32\) and the choice used.

The counts are:

| Number of factors \(m\) in 32 | Factorizations \(\binom{4}{m-1}\) | Choices for 3 | Product |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 3 | 3 |
| 2 | 4 | 5 | 20 |
| 3 | 6 | 7 | 42 |
| 4 | 4 | 9 | 36 |
| 5 | 1 | 11 | 11 |

Therefore
\[
D(96)=3+20+42+36+11=\boxed{112},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).

solutions.title: Count by the number of factors
solutions.explanation:
The factorization \(96=2^5\cdot3\) tells us that exactly one factor in any ordered product is divisible by \(3\). Choosing its position lets us count the powers of \(2\) separately.

Suppose the product has \(k\) factors. Each factor greater than \(1\) uses at least one of the six prime factors of \(96\), counted with repetition, so \(1\le k\le6\). There are \(k\) choices for the position containing \(3\).

Each of the other \(k-1\) positions must receive at least one \(2\). Assign one \(2\) to each of those positions first. We then have
\[
5-(k-1)=6-k
\]
extra twos to distribute among all \(k\) positions, allowing a position to receive none.

To count these distributions, represent the extra twos by \(6-k\) stars and use \(k-1\) bars to separate the \(k\) positions. The number of stars between bars records the extra twos in that position. Adjacent bars, or bars at the ends, allow zero extra twos. There are always
\[
(6-k)+(k-1)=5
\]
symbols, so choosing the bar positions gives \(\binom{5}{k-1}\) distributions.

For each \(k\), the count is therefore \(k\binom{5}{k-1}\). Every ordered product uniquely determines \(k\), the position containing \(3\), and the exponents of \(2\), so nothing is omitted or counted twice.

| Number of factors \(k\) | Distributions \(\binom{5}{k-1}\) | Total \(k\binom{5}{k-1}\) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 5 | 10 |
| 3 | 10 | 30 |
| 4 | 10 | 40 |
| 5 | 5 | 25 |
| 6 | 1 | 6 |

Adding the last column gives
\[
D(96)=1+10+30+40+25+6=\boxed{112},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).

solutions.title: Recur on the first factor
solutions.explanation:
Choosing the first factor leaves a smaller ordered-factorization problem. We can therefore build up the needed counts using divisors of \(96\).

For any \(n>1\), the single-factor product \(n\) contributes one representation. In every longer product, let \(d\) be the product of all factors after the first. Then \(d\) is a divisor of \(n\) with \(1<d<n\), the first factor is \(n/d\), and the remaining factors can be chosen in \(D(d)\) ways. Hence
\[
D(n)=1+\sum_{\substack{d\mid n\\1<d<n}}D(d).
\]
Different choices of \(d\) give different first factors, and every longer product has exactly one such \(d\). Thus the recurrence counts every representation once.

Apply it in increasing order. The middle column lists every divisor used in the sum; the last column is one plus the sum of their previously computed counts.

| \(n\) | Divisors used | \(D(n)\) |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | none | 1 |
| 3 | none | 1 |
| 4 | 2 | 2 |
| 6 | 2, 3 | 3 |
| 8 | 2, 4 | 4 |
| 12 | 2, 3, 4, 6 | 8 |
| 16 | 2, 4, 8 | 8 |
| 24 | 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 | 20 |
| 32 | 2, 4, 8, 16 | 16 |
| 48 | 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24 | 48 |

For example, the row for \(12\) gives
\[
D(12)=1+D(2)+D(3)+D(4)+D(6)=1+1+1+2+3=8.
\]
Finally, the proper divisors of \(96\) greater than \(1\) are \(2,3,4,6,8,12,16,24,32,48\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
D(96)&=1+1+1+2+3+4+8+8+20+16+48\\
&=\boxed{112}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
